paras: The Rock Creek assault on Eunice Martin was a reported attack on an eight-year-old Black girl by three white youths near the Twentieth street bridge over Rock Creek in Washington, D.C., in mid-July 1882. The Evening Critic and an Associated Press dispatch described it as a sexual assault that left the child in critical condition, but a police report days later said she had only been driven from a spring and stoned. Several boys were arrested and all were discharged.

According to the Critic, Louis Martin, described as an "honest and hard-working colored man," lived with his wife and daughter Eunice on the banks overlooking Rock Creek near the Twentieth street bridge.

One day in the week before July 19, Eunice was sent to a spring about 200 yards from the house and did not return when expected. Her father left his work in a nearby field to look for her, and after neighbors joined the search she was found unconscious in a heap of bushes about fifty yards from the spring. The Critic reported that a doctor dressed her wounds and that her body had been "torn and mutilated in a frightful manner." When she regained consciousness she said three boys had met her at the spring, two of them about eighteen and one about fifteen.

The case was reported to the police the day after, and Officer Cole arrested three young men whom the child could not identify. On July 21 the Critic reported that Major Brock had opened an investigation and expected arrests that day. The next day Lieutenant Johnson of the County Precinct reported to Brock that the parents' story was "incorrect": the girl had been driven from the spring and stoned by boys, but no indecent assault had occurred. A physician who examined her at Johnson's request found no signs of mutilation or abuse, and four boys who had been arrested and shown to the girl were all discharged.
No report of a trial or further arrests appears in the coverage.

The Washington Evening Critic carried the story three times, first under the headline "A Horrible Story" with the subhead "A Colored Girl, Eight Years of Age, Outraged by Three White Youths." That first article placed the case among the "horrible outrages upon children" prevalent in the District and faulted the police for assigning only one officer, asking why detectives were not put on it. After printing the police report, the paper turned its doubt on the family, remarking that it was unexplained what object the parents could have in circulating the story.

Outside Washington, the Omaha Daily Bee ran a two-sentence National Associated Press dispatch on July 20 under "Assault on a Child," calling it "an outrageous assault" by three white youths. No Black-press coverage is available for 1882, and no correction of the wire report appears in the coverage.

The nature of the attack is disputed: the family's account, carried by the Critic and the wire, described a sexual assault leaving the child unconscious and injured, while the police report, based on a physician's examination, described only a stoning. The accounts also differ on arrests, with the Critic first reporting three young men held and later four boys discharged.

bases: The papers describe an assault on one Black girl by three white youths (A2, A3), later reduced by police to a stoning by boys (A5); no mob, band or crowd is reported.
